title: Running a terminal planetarium with astroterm
excerpt: astroterm renders a real-time star map in your command line with configurable date, time and location.
body:
A quick download of the latest Linux binary and a single flag set can show the night sky over Singapore on 2 January 2025. The command below pulls the executable, makes it runnable, and runs it with the latitude and longitude for Singapore and the UTC datetime `2025-01-02T00:00:00`. The result is an ASCII map that includes the moon phase, visible planets and the surrounding constellations.

```bash
wget -O astroterm "https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-linux-x86_64" && \
chmod +x astroterm && \
./astroterm -a 1.3521 -o 103.8198 -d 2025-01-02T00:00:00
```

The repository describes astroterm as a terminal-based star map written in C. It renders real-time positions of stars, planets, constellations and lunar phases using only ASCII characters. The tool is lightweight, runs in any terminal that supports basic text output, and does not require a telescope or graphical environment. This post shows how to get astroterm on a typical platform, how to configure the view, and what the output looks like when rendering moons, planets and constellations.

## Install astroterm on your platform

The project provides several installation paths. For most Linux users, the prebuilt executable is the fastest route. The README points to a `wget` command that downloads the binary named `astroterm-linux-x86_64`. After making the file executable, it can be run directly or copied into a directory on `$PATH`.

Package managers also carry astroterm. Arch Linux users can install from the extra repository with `pacman -S astroterm`. Fedora 40+ includes the binary in its official repository, so `dnf install astroterm` works there. macOS users can pull the formula from Homebrew with `brew install astroterm`.

Nix users can start a temporary shell via  

```bash
nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command "astroterm"
```  

Guix users have a similar command using `guix shell astroterm`. If none of these match the environment, the source can be built from the `src` directory, following the guidelines in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

The download page lists the exact placeholder pattern for the URL: replace `<os>` with `linux` and `<arch>` with `x86_64` for a typical 64-bit Linux box. Windows users can fetch the `.exe` file with PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest`. All of these methods produce a single binary that runs without additional runtime dependencies.

## Configure sky view with date, time and coordinates

Astroterm accepts a handful of flags that define the observer’s location and the moment to render. The most important options are:

* `-a` or `--latitude`, observer latitude in degrees, between -90° and 90°.
* `-o` or `--longitude`, observer longitude in degrees, between -180° and 180°.
* `-d` or `--datetime`, observation time in UTC, formatted as `yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ss`.

These three flags are enough to reproduce any sky view, past or future. The example in the opening paragraph sets the latitude and longitude for Singapore and asks for the sky at midnight UTC on 2 January 2025. The tool interprets the datetime as UTC, so the local time offset is applied internally.

Additional flags let users fine-tune the rendering. `-t` controls the magnitude threshold, limiting stars to those brighter than a given value (default 5.0). `-l` sets a separate label threshold for star names (default 0.25). `-c` enables ANSI colors, while `-C` draws constellation stick figures. The `-f` flag changes the frames-per-second for animations, and `-s` scales the animation speed. All options are listed by running `astroterm --help`.

## Render moons, planets and constellations in ASCII

When invoked with the appropriate flags, astroterm prints a full-screen map. The top of the screen shows the current UTC date and time, followed by a line that lists the moon phase, the names of visible planets and their azimuth/elevation. Below that, a dense field of asterisks and other characters represents stars, with brighter stars rendered as larger symbols. If `-C` is supplied, thin lines connect the stars that belong to the same constellation, forming recognizable stick figures.

The moon phase is calculated from the supplied datetime, so the same command run for different dates will display waxing, waning or full-moon symbols. Planet positions are derived from standard ephemeris data built into the binary, giving a reasonable approximation for most amateur needs. Constellation figures are drawn only when all constituent stars meet the magnitude threshold, which prevents clutter in dense regions of the sky.

Because the output is pure ASCII, it works over SSH, inside tmux or screen sessions, and even on low-resolution terminals. The rendering speed is fast enough to animate the sky in real time; the default 24 fps provides smooth motion when the `-f` flag is left unchanged. Users who prefer a static snapshot can set `-f 1` and `-s 0` to freeze the view.

A typical run might look like this (truncated for brevity):

```text
2025-01-02 00:00:00 UTC  |  Moon: Waxing Gibbous  |  Mars 12°↑, Jupiter 45°↑
   *      *   *      *   *   *   *   *   *
  *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *
   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *
   ... (star field)
   *---*   *---*   *---*   *---*   *---*
   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *   *
```

The exact characters vary with the terminal’s font and the chosen magnitude threshold, but the overall layout remains recognizable. Users can experiment with `-t` to hide dim stars and make constellations stand out, or enable `-c` to add subtle color cues for different celestial objects.

## The takeaway

Astroterm turns any terminal into a lightweight planetarium. Install the prebuilt binary or use a package manager, then pass latitude, longitude and a UTC datetime to see moons, planets and constellations rendered in pure ASCII. The tool’s small flag set makes it easy to script sky snapshots or animate the night sky for any location and time.
